Auguste Rodin. The French sculptor who bridged the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, founding modern sculpture through psychological realism and expressive surface finish. His rough bronze castings and emotionally raw figures—The Thinker, The Kiss, The Gates of Hell—broke with neoclassical idealization and opened sculpture to modern feeling.

Rodin created The Thinker in 1880, a hunched nude pondering existence, later adopted as the symbol of philosophy and contemplation. He conceived The Gates of Hell from 1880 to 1890, a monumental bronze door inspired by Dante, from which dozens of individual figures evolved into independent works. Rodin sculpted The Kiss from 1888 to 1898, a marble pair whose intertwined intimacy scandalized conservative critics but epitomized modern sensuality.

Rodin pioneered the non-finito—deliberately rough, fragmentary bronze surfaces that suggest emerging form and raw emotion. He established the modern sculptor's studio as a laboratory, casting multiples and allowing assistants and molds to generate variations. He engaged a famous sculptural collaboration with Camille Claudel, a gifted sculptor and his lover whose own works were overshadowed by his fame. The Thinker remains his most recognizable work, now an icon of philosophy and contemplation itself.
